title: AI in Finance, Lesson 10: Writing a financial memo with AI
subtitle: From scattered data to a memo that is short, clear, and honest about its risks.
whyItMatters: A memo is what other people read and act on - your name is on it, not the AI's.
openingQuestion: What does a good financial memo need?
openingOptions: A conclusion, evidence, risks, and what still needs verifying
explanation: A financial memo is a short document that lets the reader grasp the conclusion, the evidence and the risks in a few minutes. It is the practical output of a great deal of analytical work, and it is also where AI helps most: it drafts a structured version very quickly. But an AI draft has an inherent weakness - it writes fluently even where the evidence is thin, so a confident sentence can hide a claim with no numbers behind it. Your job is to inspect every claim and cut whatever cannot be proved.

summary.keyIdea: AI helps you draft, but you have to check the figures and the risks before you send it.
summary.commonMistake: Sending the AI's version untouched, without checking sources or tone.
summary.action: Ask an AI to write a one-page memo from an article or a set of financial statements, then verify 3 of the numbers yourself.

sections.text: A memo is a short written record that helps the reader make a decision or know what to check next.

sections.label: Terminology
sections.text: Memo: a short memorandum. One-pager: a single-page document. Investment thesis: the central argument for why you should or should not invest.
Using the information below, write a one-page memo. Include: Conclusion, Evidence, Risks, Missing data, Questions to verify. Do not invent figures.
Check the sources of the figures, the units, the risks and the tone. What goes out is your responsibility, not the AI's.

sections.title: The five-part frame and what counts as done

concepts.def: Two to three sentences at most, stating plainly what you believe and how confident you are. If the reader has only 2 minutes, this section has to be enough.
Three main claims, each with a figure and a source. Without a number it is an opinion, not evidence.
The two largest risks, written specifically enough that the reader knows what to watch. Avoid generic risks like 'market volatility'.
Information you need but do not have. This section makes the memo more credible rather than weaker.
Concrete actions: which note to look up, who to ask, which metric to track next quarter.

sections.label: A full prompt you can reuse
sections.text: "Working entirely from the data I provide below, write a memo of at most 500 words in exactly these 5 sections: Conclusion (2-3 sentences), Evidence (3 claims, each one required to carry a figure and a source), Risks (2 specific risks), Missing data, What to do next. Do not use evaluative adjectives unless a figure accompanies them. Do not give a buy or sell recommendation. If a section has insufficient data, say so explicitly instead of writing something generic."
Three review passes before you send

items: Pass 1 - The figures: reopen the source, check each number against it, check the units and the reporting period.
Pass 2 - The claims: underline every evaluative adjective, ask 'which number proves this?', and cut whatever cannot answer.
Pass 3 - The reader: give it to somebody who knows nothing about the business, let them read for 2 minutes, then ask them to summarise the conclusion and the risks back to you.

sections.text: If the reader in pass 3 summarises it wrongly, the problem is in the memo, not in the reader. A good memo is not the best-written one but the hardest one to misunderstand.

lines: AI drafts fast; you are what makes it trustworthy.
A good memo is one that helps the reader know what to ask next.

quiz.question: What does a memo mean here?
options: A table of daily share prices for a list of stocks
A full statutory audit report on the annual accounts
A short internal memorandum written to be read in minutes
A signed loan agreement between a bank and a borrower
quiz.explanation: A memo is simply a short written note circulated internally so a decision-maker can absorb a position quickly. It is not a price table, which carries data but no argument; it is not an audit report, which is a formal opinion issued by a licensed firm on a full set of statements; and it is not a contract, which creates legal obligations between parties rather than presenting an analytical view.

quiz.question: What must you do before sending a draft written by AI?
options: Ask the AI whether the draft is rigorous enough already
Polish the wording so it reads more smoothly still
Add a chart to illustrate the conclusion section
Check the sources, figures, units and risks
quiz.explanation: The AI drafts; the person who sends it owns the quality. Asking the model to grade its own work returns the same confidence that produced the draft, so it detects nothing. Polishing the prose makes a weak claim read better rather than making it true. And a chart adds a presentation layer on top of numbers you have not yet verified - which is the wrong order of work.

quiz.question: Why does a 'missing data' section make a memo more credible?
options: Because it tells the reader where the boundary of the conclusion lies
Because it proves you have read every single one of the original documents
Because it makes the memo longer and more complete to look at
Because it is a mandatory section under the reporting standards
quiz.explanation: A conclusion that states what it rests on and what it does not yet know is one that can be checked. A conclusion that looks absolutely certain has usually hidden the unknown part. Naming gaps proves nothing about how much you read, length is not a virtue in a memo, and no reporting standard governs an internal memo's sections.

quiz.question: What is the fastest way to spot an unsupported claim in an AI draft?
options: Read the draft backwards from the very last paragraph to the first one
Underline every evaluative adjective and ask which figure proves it
Count how many times the draft mentions the name of the business
Have a second AI rewrite it and then compare the two versions
quiz.explanation: Evaluative adjectives - 'positive', 'leading', 'improving', 'sustainable' - are exactly where a judgement slips in among the facts. If there is a number, keep it; if there is not, cut it. Reading backwards is a different technique for a different problem, counting name mentions measures nothing, and a second model produces a second fluent draft rather than a check.

quiz.question: What is a quick way to check a memo written by AI?
options: Compare its length against the memos written in earlier periods
Read it start to finish to check the whole argument hangs together
Read backwards from the conclusion, asking what evidence each sentence rests on
Ask the AI to rate how confident it is in each section it just wrote
quiz.explanation: Reading forwards lets the fluency of the prose carry you along. Reading backwards forces every assertion to stand on its own evidence, and the sentences with nothing underneath them show up immediately. Length comparisons say nothing about substance, a coherence check rewards smooth writing, and a self-rating comes from the same model that wrote the unsupported sentence.

diagram.label: AI drafts against the five-part frame
You inspect each claim: is there evidence yet?
Cut what cannot be proved → the version you send

realWorldExample.company: A confident sentence hiding a weak claim
realWorldExample.description: One sentence pattern shows up constantly in AI drafts: 'With its industry-leading position and improving margins, the business has a positive growth outlook over the medium term.' It reads beautifully, and it contains three claims with no evidence: leading by what criterion and on whose numbers, margins improving from what level to what level, and how long 'medium term' is. The simple test: underline every evaluative adjective in the draft, then for each one ask 'which figure proves this?'. Any sentence that cannot answer gets a number added or gets deleted.

keyTakeaways: The five-part frame: conclusion, evidence, risks, missing data, next steps.
The 'missing data' section is what earns credibility - do not drop it to make the memo look more certain.
Underline every evaluative adjective and demand a figure; if there is no number, cut it.
Re-check the draft's figures against the original source before sending - the responsibility is yours.

practicePrompt.question: What does a good financial memo need?
options: A conclusion, evidence, risks, and what still needs verifying
Only praise
Only pretty icons
No figures needed
practicePrompt.explanation: A good memo has to let the reader understand both the conclusion and what it rests on.

application.title: Practise it now
application.message: Ask an AI to write a one-page memo from an article or a set of financial statements, then verify 3 of the numbers yourself.
application.secondary: Start small, verify clearly, and only then raise the difficulty.
